title: How to build a personal brand (full course)
creator: Caleb Ralston
one_liner: Branding is an intentional pairing of relevant things done consistently; build trust first, and everything else scales.
why_it_matters: Most small creators post randomly and hope something sticks, which is Caleb's 'forgettable brand' path. This course gives you the whole system above the edit: what to be known for, what to refuse, which topics, which platforms, how often to post, how to read your numbers, and how trust turns into money later. At ~930 followers you are early enough to set these choices on purpose instead of fixing them in two years.

chapters.title: 1. What brand and branding are
chapters.summary: Caleb opens with two paths. Path one is the forgettable brand: you post randomly, people don't know who you are, so they don't engage or buy. Path two is the intentional brand: you own what people associate with you and your content moves them toward a decision. He then defines his terms. Branding is a pairing of things; good branding is an intentional pairing of relevant things done consistently; brand is the byproduct, the association the audience draws without being told. His examples are Nike paired with Michael Jordan (athletic greatness), Gary Vaynerchuk paired with content, and Harley-Davidson paired with freedom. The point is that this makes brand something you can actually do rather than 'woo woo' magic.

blocks.title: The two paths he opens with

left.title: Forgettable brand
items: Posts content randomly, hoping something sticks
People have no idea who you are or what you do
So they don't engage, and they definitely don't buy

right.title: Intentional brand
items: You own what people associate with you
Content builds trust and moves people toward a decision
If you're already here, the course is about breaking your ceiling

blocks.title: Caleb's definition of brand

items.label: Intentional
items.text: You choose the pairing on purpose instead of letting it happen.

items.label: Relevant
items.text: The thing you pair with fits where you want to go (Jordan for a basketball brand).

items.label: Consistent
items.text: You do it again and again; one post is not a pairing.

items.label: Brand
items.text: The audience now associates you with that thing by itself.

blocks.caption: Branding = a pairing of things. Good branding = intentional + relevant + consistent. Brand = the association that results.

blocks.text: I define good branding as an intentional pairing of relevant things done consistently
It takes all of the woo woo fluffy magic out of what brand is and it makes it something that you can actually do.

blocks.title: Applied: the pairing test on your feed
blocks.before: A gym PR one day, a GPU unboxing the next, a ranked clip after that, each with a different tone and no thread tying them to you.
blocks.after: Every post pairs 'Srijan' with the same thing: unhinged humour on top of real competence (heavy lifts, clean builds, actual game sense), so the topics change but the feeling doesn't.
blocks.why: An association only forms when the same pairing repeats. Caleb's three ingredients: intentional, relevant, consistent.

chapters.title: 2. Define your brand: work backwards, then choose associations
chapters.summary: Your brand exists whether you define it or not; if you don't, your audience defines it for you. Caleb's Brand Journey Framework works backwards from the end goal in four questions: desired outcome, what you must be known for, what you must do to be known for it, and what you must learn to do it. The last question gives you day-one actions. He claims almost nobody posting knows what they are trying to accomplish. Next come associations: what should people think of when they hear your name? Then the question he calls more important and says almost everyone ignores: what do you NOT want to be associated with? 'Intentional' isn't the same as 'good': if you keep appearing on podcasts or in collabs with scammy people, the audience pairs you with them, so he would turn down even the biggest show.

blocks.title: The Brand Journey Framework (start at the top, act from the bottom)

items.label: 1. Desired outcome
items.text: What do I want to have happen?

items.label: 2. Known for
items.text: What do I have to be known for in order for that to happen?

items.label: 3. Do
items.text: What do I have to do to be known for that? Brand is actions, not just words.

items.label: 4. Learn
items.text: What do I have to learn to do that? This rung is today's to-do list.

blocks.caption: Read it top to bottom to plan. Live it bottom to top: learn → do → become known → outcome.

blocks.title: Alice and the Cheshire Cat
blocks.text: Alice reaches a fork in the road and asks the cat which way to go. The cat asks where she is trying to end up. She says she doesn't know, so the cat says either road will take her there. Caleb's point: without a desired outcome, you still go somewhere, just maybe not where you wanted.

blocks.label: of people posting have no idea what they're trying to accomplish
blocks.note: He uses the same figure for people who ignore anti-associations. It is a rhetorical number, not a study.

blocks.title: Applied: associations vs anti-associations for a gym + tech + gaming creator

left.title: Pair with (on purpose)
items: Real progress you can show: lifts, builds, ranks
Humour that still teaches something
Honest gear and supplement opinions
Creators whose audience trusts them

right.title: Refuse (even for reach)
items: Sponsors you'd never use: sketchy supplements, betting or 'trading' apps
Collabs with rage-bait or scammy 'giveaway' pages
Fake-review deals for PC parts
Content that only works by punching down

blocks.text: If you don't actively shape your associations, your audience is going to do it for you.

Intentional doesn't mean right. You can be very consistent about pairing yourself with the wrong things, and the audience will still draw that association. Caleb's rule for collabs and podcasts: if your gut says no, the exposure isn't worth it, because awareness is not worth the trade.

chapters.title: 3. Position your brand: own the gap
chapters.summary: Positioning means not blending in: find what's missing in your space and fill it, whether that's information, a philosophy or simply your personality reaching people others don't. His own gap: others push virality and views, he pushes a long-term trust-built brand, because when the algorithm changes nobody searches for the name of someone who only chased views. Your story is the differentiator, so tell stories instead of claiming traits. Mine your comments for objections and answer them inside the content, like a good video sales letter. Don't be a robot: share losses, not only wins. Finally, listen to your audience (and friends, early on) for what they praise you for, and let feedback change how you present your beliefs, not the beliefs themselves.

blocks.title: Five positioning moves

items.label: Find the gap
items.text: What is missing in your space: information, philosophy, or personality/unique take?

items.label: Tell your story
items.text: List pivotal moments, challenges overcome, turning points, unique experiences. Show, don't claim.

items.label: Answer objections in the content
items.text: Read comments for 'does this work for me?' doubts and answer them before they're asked.

items.label: Don't be a robot
items.text: Bring your personality; share losses and the lessons from them.

items.label: Listen, but don't become a politician
items.text: Let feedback shape how you present ideas (add context), not what you believe.

blocks.caption: Two gap questions: what are creators in my space saying that I disagree with? How can I bring a fresh perspective to what's been taught for years?

blocks.title: Tell the story, don't claim the trait
blocks.after: When editing Gary Vee's Trash Talk series I worked 12–14 hours a day Sunday to Thursday, then came in at 6 a.m. Thursday and didn't leave until 2 p.m. Friday: about 32 hours straight.
blocks.why: Nobody cares about tropes like 'hardworking' or 'innovative'; they remember the story behind it. Same with Bezos using a door as a desk instead of saying 'resourceful'.

blocks.text: I actually think that losses are more relatable than wins.

blocks.title: The client everyone thought was a robot
blocks.text: A creator he worked with came across as pure information with no personality, and her audience thought she wasn't human. In real life she was hilarious and quirky, and people who met her said she was much nicer and funnier than expected. His first goal was to get that side into the content. Lesson: bring your whole self, because nobody else is like you.

His rule for comments: if you ignore the praise, you can ignore the hate. If you get high on applause, the hateful comments will crush you. The useful middle is the real signal: what people repeatedly praise you for (for him, ~90% of client calls ended with comments on his energy) is what you lean into on camera.

Your likely gap: most gym and PC creators are either polished and serious or pure meme pages. 'Unhinged but actually knows the lift / the build' sits between them. Test it with Caleb's question: what do the big gym and tech accounts say that you disagree with? (e.g. 'you need a ₹2 lakh rig for 1440p', 'never skip leg day' delivered with zero humour).

chapters.title: 4. The brand story framework
chapters.summary: Caleb rejects the common problem → transformation → outcome story as too rigid: it assumes one dramatic aha moment, that the founder story is the most important one, and that a brand never evolves. Great brands are built on consistency, distinction and connecting with the right audience over time. His three-part framework is Catalyst (why your brand exists), Core truth (what makes you different: a conviction you share publicly, not controversy for its own sake) and Proof (repeated evidence through actions). Each part has three questions. He illustrates core truth with the musician Russ (artists should stay independent and own their music) and proof with Gary Vee proving content volume for 15+ years. Nail all three and your brand has loyalty, not just a story.

blocks.title: Why he drops the classic story framework

left.title: Problem → transformation → outcome
items: Assumes one dramatic aha moment
Assumes the founder story matters most
Assumes the brand never evolves
Too narrow for most real brands

right.title: Catalyst → core truth → proof
items: Works when the start was an opportunity, not a struggle
Built on consistency and distinction over time
Proof keeps growing as you keep doing things
Leads to loyalty, not just a nice origin tale

blocks.title: The three-part brand story

items.label: Catalyst
items.text: Why the brand exists: something needed to change, or a gap/opportunity you saw.

items.label: Core truth
items.text: What you believe that others don't, shared publicly. Not controversy for controversy's sake.

items.label: Proof
items.text: What you do and show over and over: case studies, results, a pattern of credibility.

items.label: Loyalty
items.text: The result when all three are clear and repeated.

blocks.caption: His own version: catalyst = brands chased views but couldn't build trust; core truth = brand is intentional pairing, not virality; proof = brands he scaled, and he shows how for free.

blocks.title: The nine questions
items: Catalyst: What needs to change?
Catalyst: What do you see that others don't?
Catalyst: Why do you feel the need to act on it?
Core truth: What do I believe that others do not?
Core truth: What about my personality stands out (what do people compliment)?
Core truth: Why would the audience care, and what value does it bring them?
Proof: How does every piece of content reinforce the associations I want?
Proof: What case studies or examples establish my credibility?
Proof: If someone hears my name, what's the first thing they think of?

blocks.text: your brand is not what you say, it's what you do and prove over and over again.

blocks.title: Russ: a core truth lived out loud
blocks.text: The musician Russ believes artists should stay independent and own the rights to their music, for creative control and more profit. He puts that belief in his songs and repeats it in podcasts and news interviews. That repetition of one conviction is what Caleb means by a core truth.

Draft yours with prompts, not invented facts. Catalyst: what annoyed you about gym/tech content before you started? Core truth: one belief you'd defend (e.g. 'fitness and tech content can be stupid-funny and still correct'). Proof: what you can keep showing every month (your lifts going up, builds that actually run, ranked progress, your follower count climbing from ~930).

chapters.title: 5. Picking your topics
chapters.summary: Start narrow: early trust comes from being great at one specific thing and talking about it obsessively, like the friend who only talks about woodworking (believed) versus the friend who's 'best at everything' (believed at nothing). Gary Vee was 'the wine guy' on Wine Library TV for years before expanding to marketing. Expand only when you're truly excellent at the new topic, when the current topic gets consistent engagement, into adjacent topics, or when the audience asks about something you've hinted at. Keep your roots as you grow (Amazon + Audible, Crayola bringing back retired colours, Knocked Loose still playing old songs), and expand in layers, not leaps. Pillars are guidelines, not rules: his Harley videos aren't a pillar but make him more interesting. Spend about 80% on your core subject and 20% on other interests, which he calls interest stacking.

blocks.text: early trust is built off of being great at one specific thing and talking about that same specific thing.

blocks.title: When to expand into a new topic

items.label: You're actually excellent at it
items.text: Don't teach what you don't know well yet.

items.label: The current topic is working
items.text: Consistent engagement and positive feedback on what you're known for.

items.label: It's adjacent
items.text: Brand strategy → breathwork is a leap; inch toward it instead.

items.label: The audience asks for it
items.text: They want more of something you've hinted at or shown in passing.

blocks.caption: Pro tip: expand in layers, not leaps. And keep returning to your roots now and then for the day-one fans.

blocks.label: core subject / other interests
blocks.note: 80% on what you want to be known for (ideally tied to your offer), 20% on interests that make you human. Not a hard rule.

blocks.title: Applied: your interest stack

items.label: Gym
items.text: Lifting, physique, gym culture and its jokes.

items.label: Tech / PC
items.text: Builds, parts, setups, iPhone filming tricks.

items.label: Gaming
items.text: Ranked grind, game takes, setup performance.

blocks.caption: Each circle is another 'at bat' for a viewer to think 'I like that too'. The overlaps (gaming PC + gym discipline, gym nerd who benchmarks his rig) are the rare intersection nobody else owns. Pick which one is your 80%.

blocks.text: somebody who loves human optimization and making their body healthier, but they're also a complete computer science nerd. That is a very interesting intersection.

blocks.title: The co-worker who also loves Kendrick
blocks.text: On day one you share only one thing with co-workers: the company. Then you mention you're a huge Kendrick Lamar fan during the Drake beef, and Sarah says she is too. Now you share two things, you become work friends, and maybe real friends later. More interests in your content give the audience more of those moments. Joe Rogan does this: like one of his topics and you might watch; like three or four and you're a superfan.

chapters.title: 6. Choosing your content medium
chapters.summary: The content section starts with a training analogy: a good personal trainer doesn't put a beginner on Ronnie Coleman's programme, because the best routine is the one you'll stick with. So don't copy MrBeast's volume or production on day one. There are four mediums: written, video, audio and visual/graphic. He suggests doing all of them eventually but picking one as your '80%'. Video is the highest-leverage medium because one shoot feeds clips, podcast audio, quote graphics, written posts and stills. If video terrifies you, a podcast is a stepping stone. If you ramble ('bunny brain'), get a better editor rather than quitting video, and if your voice is monotone, make that your bit.

blocks.title: The four mediums by what they ask of you

items.label: Written
items.text: LinkedIn, X, Facebook, newsletters, articles. Value per sentence; must make sense without you saying it out loud.

items.label: Visual / graphic
items.text: Infographics, carousels, PDF carousels on LinkedIn. Canva/Figma make novices look intermediate; simpler is better.

items.label: Audio
items.text: Podcasts. No camera fear, but no visuals either, so your words must paint the picture. Cadence changes act as pattern interrupts.

items.label: Video
items.text: YouTube long and short, TikTok, Reels, LinkedIn video, Spotify video. Highest leverage: one shoot feeds every other medium.

blocks.caption: Our 2×2 arrangement of his four mediums. Pick the one you can do for years as your 80%.

blocks.title: Is video your 80%? (his self-check)
items: Are you comfortable on camera, or at least willing to improve in public over time?
Can you handle negative feedback about how you talk or how entertaining you are?
Do you get excited about visuals and grabbing attention?
Can you speak concisely without rambling, or are you OK learning that on the job?

blocks.text: Video content is the highest leverage medium that you can engage in.

blocks.title: Written vs video, in his words

left.title: Written
items: Think 'value per sentence'
If you have to explain the post, throw it in the trash
He rewrites a LinkedIn post ~10 times minimum
Feb 2025: LinkedIn comments show your post to the commenter's network ('true virality')

right.title: Video
items: Think 'value per second'
One long video → shorts, podcast audio, quote posts, transcript-based written posts, stills
Rambling ('bunny brain') = get a better editor, not a reason to quit
If it fills you with dread, start with audio and come back

blocks.label: carousels were 'murdering' on Instagram; photos of real hand-drawn things worked well
blocks.note: Platform observations from the filming date, ~20 months before this module. Re-check before relying on them.

blocks.text: Your 80% is almost certainly video (iPhone 15 + tripod, funny delivery). Use his voice tip: speed up then slow down, go loud then quiet, to flag the important line. And his 'turn the weakness into your bit' idea fits an unhinged persona: whatever feels like a flaw on camera can become the running joke.

chapters.title: 7. Choosing your platforms
chapters.summary: Prioritise two or three platforms rather than posting everywhere, so you aren't exposed to single-platform risk (his example: TikTok vanished in the US for about 12 hours a month before filming, and people whose income lived only there panicked). Among those, use the 'Eye of Sauron': focus resources on one while the others sit in maintenance mode, then rotate. Start where you're comfortable and already spend time, scroll it strategically and take notes, and post where you believe your audience is, treating that as a hypothesis you test by watching for leads. Short form is for awareness; long form is where conversion happens, because time spent with you raises willingness to act. Look at results, not ego, and optimise for conversions (sales, streams, hires) over vanity metrics, because a small correct audience beats a big wrong one.

blocks.title: The Eye of Sauron rotation

items.label: Focus on platform A
items.text: Most effort and growth goal here.

items.label: B and C in maintenance
items.text: Post enough to keep the current audience engaged; growth is a bonus.

items.label: A reaches maintenance level
items.text: You've built the habit and system there.

items.label: Rotate the eye to B
items.text: Now B gets the focus while A and C maintain.

blocks.caption: Two or three platforms total, one in focus at a time. He admits he runs four: 'Do more of what I say in this, not as much of what I do.'

blocks.title: Applied: where to start (built from his platform questions)

axes.x: Your comfort / time spent there: low → high
axes.y: Your audience is there: unlikely → likely

items.label: Learn it later
items.text: Audience likely there but you're not comfortable yet. Study it by scrolling with notes before committing.

items.label: Start here
items.text: You already live on it and your people are there (Instagram Reels / YouTube Shorts for gym + tech + gaming).

items.label: Skip for now
items.text: Neither your habit nor your audience. Don't spread thin.

items.label: Maintenance only
items.text: Comfortable but not your audience. Fine to post, don't pour effort in.

blocks.caption: Our 2×2 from his questions: where do you spend your time, and where do you believe your audience is? Treat the second as a hypothesis and test it.

blocks.text: I view long form as the place where conversion actually happens.

blocks.title: The Harley dealership's waiting game
blocks.text: When you buy a Harley, the finance team runs your credit in seconds but makes you sit and chat for 10–15 minutes, then gives you a tour of the dealership. The goal is to get you to invest time so you feel you might as well complete the purchase. Caleb sees long-form content the same way: the more time your audience spends with you, the more likely they are to convert.

blocks.label: followers: people he knows making millions a year
blocks.note: Versus people with millions of followers who make very little. His own 68K Instagram came from landscape photography ~10 years ago and doesn't engage with his current topic. He'd take 30–40% fewer likes/views for a higher conversion rate.

blocks.text: Myth: you need to look and sound perfect before posting. Caleb admits watching the course footage made him feel he 'looks fat', and says if he let ego decide, none of the content would be out. Look at the metrics and engagement, not the little voice about how your voice sounds.

chapters.title: 8. Posting cadence and the accordion method
chapters.summary: Caleb reframes quality vs quantity. Nobody, including you, knows what 'quality' is in advance; your audience decides it through views, likes and comments. Volume is a tool for getting that data faster: 10 videos in a week teach you more quickly than 10 videos over a month. That's the accordion: expand volume to learn, then compress and put more effort into each piece based on what the audience called quality. Start with your highest-leverage platform (most results, and the most repurposable content, usually long form), track off-platform conversions, and don't withhold posts because you think they're not good enough. Perfect is the enemy of posted: pick a cadence you can sustain, even weekly or every other week.

blocks.title: The accordion method

items.label: Expand
items.text: Post more, even lightly edited ('just trimmed'), to gather signals fast.

items.label: Read the signals
items.text: What got more views, likes, comments, questions? That's what your audience calls quality.

items.label: Compress
items.text: Fewer pieces, more effort each, built on what they picked (effort of 5 videos into 1).

items.label: Expand again
items.text: When results stall or the platform shifts, open up to learn again.

blocks.caption: He also uses the accordion for careers: wide, then narrow and specialised, then wide again.

blocks.text: Your audience is who determines what quality is, not you.
Some of the most viral videos, most viewed and engaged with videos ever online are filmed at night in the dark on a cell phone.

blocks.title: His cadence rules
items: Start with the highest-leverage platform: most results, and content you can repurpose the most (usually long form).
Track off-platform conversions and double down where they come from.
Early on, raise volume for speed of learning, not just reach.
Don't make the decision for your audience by sitting on 'not good enough' posts.
Perfect is the enemy of posted: daily is unrealistic for most; try 3×/week, weekly or every other week.
Whatever you pick, it must be sustainable. Don't squat 800 lb when you've never squatted 135.

blocks.title: YouTube had the most leads; LinkedIn converted best
blocks.text: On one team, YouTube was #1 for absolute leads, Instagram #2, LinkedIn #3. But by percentage of audience converting, LinkedIn was #1 'by a mile', because it was a smaller audience that had been an afterthought. They moved resources there, at one point spending probably $20–30K a month on LinkedIn organic alone, and saw big returns.

blocks.label: of consistent posting puts you in the 'top 1%'
blocks.note: His claim: most people give up after a week or two. He posts ~1 long-form video a month himself, because 2,000+ business Q&As already told him what people want.

chapters.title: 9. Increasing volume: pillar content, the waterfall, the top 10%
chapters.summary: Once you're consistent, increase output from one pillar piece (a long YouTube video, deep thread, long LinkedIn post or newsletter) by 'mining' it for gold: self-contained paragraphs, quotes, a short summary, or clips with a slightly contrarian or nuanced take. He calls this the waterfall distribution model and credits Gary Vee. One YouTube video becomes clips, quote posts, a LinkedIn post (also used on Facebook and as an Instagram reel caption) and carousels: 'easily over 10 pieces'. Scale one platform at a time, and in Feb 2025 he preferred more effort per post over more posts, because a 1M-view video reaches new people while four 250K videos mostly reach the existing audience. Finally, review your top 10% every month and copy only what all of them share.

blocks.title: Waterfall: one YouTube video, live-mined

items.label: Short clips
items.text: Editors clip the strongest moments (contrarian or nuanced) for Reels, TikTok, Shorts.

items.label: Quotes
items.text: Punchy lines from the transcript for Threads / X, or as image posts.

items.label: Written post
items.text: Rewrite a transcript moment into a LinkedIn post; post it on Facebook too.

items.label: Caption reuse
items.text: Use that written post as the caption of one of the Instagram clips.

items.label: Carousels
items.text: Two slides per section of the video (listicle videos work best).

blocks.caption: 'Easily over 10 pieces of content' from one video. Later (chapter 10) he qualifies it: by 2025, native-per-platform beats pure clipping.

blocks.title: Carousel rules (Feb 2025)
items: Two slides per section of the source video.
One very basic, easy-to-understand image plus one or two sentences at most per slide.
Slides 1 AND 2 both carry a hook (reinterpret the video's hook): Instagram re-serves the carousel to non-engagers starting at slide 2.
Listicles ('10 things I learned…') suit carousels best; for a complex deep dive, carousel just one section.
This is an observation, not a rule.

blocks.label: same views, not the same eyeballs
blocks.note: His client's four videos a month averaged ~250K, but 60–70% of those views came from the existing audience; one 1M video reaches mostly new people. He notes MrBeast posted every 4–8 weeks.

blocks.text: it's the same number of views. It's not the same number of eyeballs.

items.label: Take the window
items.text: Last 90 days of posts (or 30 if that's all you have).

items.label: Pull the top 10%
items.text: Your best performers on that platform.

items.label: Find what's in ALL of them
items.text: Usually only one, maybe two things. If it's in only one or two posts, it's a crapshoot.

items.label: Put it in every next post
items.text: Learn from the top, never from the bottom 10–20%.

items.label: Repeat monthly
items.text: Even when 'nothing is performing', some posts beat others. Keep laddering up.

blocks.text: Two ways to scale a platform: more posts or more effort per post. His Feb 2025 stance: take the effort of five posts and put it into three. He says 'lower volume' instead of 'higher quality' because quality is the audience's call, not his.

chapters.title: 10. Making content sustainable
chapters.summary: Content only pays off if you keep doing it for years, so don't force a medium you hate. Build a simple content machine: a baseline like one YouTube video every two weeks plus three shorts a week, held for 2–3 months before raising it. Batching works for some, but he often sees a 12-hour batch day add pressure that hurts performance. Remove yourself from execution as soon as you can afford help, and make the team responsible for the talent's environment: nods and thumbs-ups while filming, fist bumps between takes, a skeptic's pass for objections, and an honest message after the shoot. Repurposing is a good start, but by 2025 content should be contextual to each platform, and the best repurposing uses what worked on one platform to inform a new medium elsewhere. Film at your best-energy time and protect content time like an important meeting.

blocks.text: Content creation should be sustainable for years, not months.

blocks.title: The talent-environment playbook (the parts he shared)

items.label: Visual feedback while filming
items.text: The videographer nods, harder as the point gets better, and gives a thumbs up. It tells the talent 'go deeper here'.

items.label: Fist bump between takes
items.text: Plus one or two specific things that stood out. It keeps energy and momentum up.

items.label: Think like a skeptic ('2.0')
items.text: After each section, ask what the audience will doubt or ask, and add that context, like a good sales video.

items.label: Message 15–20 min after
items.text: Honest, never fake, naming 1–2 content points. Film days become associated with good feelings.

blocks.caption: Principle: it is the team's job, not the creator's, to create the right environment. The audience's feedback loop is slow (this course dropped 6+ weeks after filming), so on-set feedback matters.

blocks.title: Repurposing 2.0: one tweet's journey (client case)

items.label: Tweet
items.text: A strong statement becomes one of her most-liked tweets ever: that's social listening.

items.label: Short
items.text: The tweet is the hook; she explains the story behind it.

items.label: Poster photo
items.text: The quote printed as a poster, photographed in a nice setting: her top Instagram post.

items.label: LinkedIn post
items.text: Same hook, expanded with more commentary: a top-3 post.

items.label: YouTube video
items.text: 25–30 min video titled from the quote: in her top 10.

blocks.caption: They never reposted the tweet everywhere; they remade it for each platform's needs.

blocks.title: The 'you are you' analogy
blocks.before: The same clip, same caption, same hook pushed to every app at the same time.
blocks.after: Same message, re-told per platform. Sarah is still Sarah at Saturday brunch with family, cocktails that night and a Monday business meeting, but she changes topics, tone and vocabulary for each.
blocks.why: That isn't inauthentic; it's knowing your audience. Platforms are different events.

blocks.title: Simple content machine
items: Set a baseline you can hit (his example: 1 YouTube video every 2 weeks + 3 shorts a week on Instagram and YouTube Shorts).
Hold it for 2–3 months, then raise the bar.
Batching is optional: a 12-hour film day can create pressure that hurts the delivery. Align the plan with your real calendar.
Film at your best-energy time of day (his: mornings).
Protect content time like an important business meeting; constant rescheduling tells your helpers it isn't a priority.

blocks.text: Solo with a tripod you have no one nodding. Fake the loop: film with a gym buddy behind the phone who reacts, or do a quick playback after each take and mark the 1–2 lines that actually landed. And note his aside: photos of real-world things (a printed quote, a post-it, a drawing) were doing well, which suits a whiteboard 'split' or a hand-drawn PC build diagram.

chapters.title: 11. Storytelling, story types, and why education is scaling trust
chapters.summary: Stories change perspectives, keep attention, build emotional connection and are remembered better than facts; even MrBeast added more storytelling (Beast Games). His framework is Hook → Problem → Journey → Lesson → CTA, meant to be used fluidly. Hooks get 2–3 seconds on short form and 15–20 seconds max on YouTube long form, and work best as a bold or contrarian statement, a pattern interrupt or a thought-provoking question (unexpected facts are 'getting a little tiresome'). The best story types are origin, failure (with the lesson), success, client success and contrarian industry stories. Then the key idea of the course: pair yourself with success stories, people trust you, act on your lessons, get results, and start associating you with their own success, so your offer later looks cheap next to its value.

blocks.title: The storytelling framework (flexible, not rigid)

items.label: Hook
items.text: Bold/contrarian statement, pattern interrupt, or thought-provoking question. E.g. 'Subscribers, views, likes don't matter. What actually matters is…'

items.label: Problem
items.text: Set the stakes. Specific and relatable, not necessarily dramatic: 'I was working 14 hours a day for my hero, Gary Vaynerchuk, but I still felt stuck.'

items.label: Journey
items.text: How you overcame it, low points included. Show the messy middle and your doubt.

items.label: Lesson
items.text: Make it useful: step-by-step, chunked down, something they can do immediately. Tie it to your expertise or offer.

items.label: CTA
items.text: Just 'take action', not necessarily 'buy'. E.g. comment your biggest takeaway and how you'll apply it.

blocks.caption: 'You now have the rules. Feel free to break the rules.'

blocks.label: to win attention on short form
blocks.note: YouTube long form: about 15–20 s max (the industry says 30 s). Viewers check: is this what I clicked on, and is this the person I want to hear it from?

blocks.title: The blueberry clip
blocks.text: One of the most viral clips Caleb ever made for Gary Vee opens with Gary chomping blueberries: 'I eat blueberries like it's my job.' Then: 'You missed the first 30 I ate.' It was such a pattern interrupt that it became Gary's most viral clip at the time.

items.label: Origin
items.text: Resonates most. Keep retelling it: treat every post as if it reaches a cold audience. Where you are now isn't relatable; how you got there is.

items.label: Failure
items.text: People trust vulnerability more than success. Not a sob story: give the lesson so they avoid the cost. (His: tripled income, then pay cut in half, had to fire three friends.)

items.label: Success
items.text: Before/after and small wins that became big results, as proof. (His claim: Gary Vee's TikTok 300K → 3.5M in 3 months.)

items.label: Client / customer success
items.text: Proof you can replicate it for others; viewers see themselves in it.

items.label: Industry (contrarian)
items.text: State the trope everyone treats as gospel, then your contrary view, respectfully, no names.

blocks.title: Educational content = scaling trust

items.label: Pair with success stories
items.text: Consistently share wins: yours and others'.

items.label: Association
items.text: The audience links you with success.

items.label: Trust
items.text: They trust what you say, so they hear the lessons.

items.label: Action → results
items.text: They act on the lessons and get their own outcome.

items.label: Their success
items.text: Now they associate you with THEIR success: whatever they invest with you returns more.

items.label: Offer
items.text: When you present one, it feels small next to the value they expect.

blocks.caption: His seminar example: buyers told sales to just take their card; he claims $1,000 tickets delivered 50–100× the value (his claim).

blocks.text: Ultimately, educational content is just scaling trust.

chapters.title: 12. Community-driven content
chapters.summary: Involve your audience in what you make: post two versions (of a verse, a chapter, a title) and let them choose, and they become invested 'missionaries'. The shift is from creator-first to community-first. The best ideas come from the audience, but from DM and comment questions, not 'what should I make next?' polls, which are too open-ended. Gary Vee's social listening: if five people ask the same thing in a few hours, thousands have that question, so answer it immediately (without saying 'so many of you asked'). Make the audience the hero by sharing their wins publicly, and stitch their UGC. To turn viewers into members: make engagement the goal, reply to and reward the people already commenting, and build inside jokes and shared language.

blocks.text: The mindset shift here is shifting from creator first to community first.

blocks.title: Where good ideas actually come from

left.title: Weak: open polls
items: 'What should I make next?'
Way too open ('blue ocean'), no constraints
People don't know what they need

right.title: Strong: questions they already ask
items: DM questions
Comment questions
5 people asking the same thing in ~3 hours = thousands wondering it right now
Answer fast, don't announce 'so many of you asked'

blocks.title: Three pillars of community content

items.label: Educational
items.text: Solve their biggest problems.

items.label: Conversational
items.text: Make them feel heard; two-way, not talking at them.

items.label: Social proof
items.text: Showcase community wins and real stories.

blocks.caption: Use the pillars to generate more ideas. Example of social proof: record an Instagram video call with someone who DM'd you a win. It won't be a top performer, but it invites more success stories.

items.label: Make engagement the goal
items.text: Ask for a fire emoji if it helped, or invite debate on a counter-norm take ('I'll be in the comments arguing with some of you').

items.label: Respond and reward participation
items.text: Most people asking how to grow engagement aren't replying to the three people already commenting.

items.label: Inside jokes and shared language
items.text: Use the niche's existing lingo or create your own.

blocks.text: His own example is your niche: 'gym bros have bulking season'. Build a lexicon across your three worlds (bulking season / 'it's always the RAM' / 'skill issue') and invent one recurring phrase that's yours. Then reply to every comment for a month; at ~930 followers that's very doable and it's exactly the signal he says newcomers look for.
UGC loop: prompt viewers to post their own story or result from your lesson, then stitch or duet them. 'No audience is too small': he wants even 300-follower accounts telling their people about him.

chapters.title: 13. Scaling your content: native editors and the multiplier sheet
chapters.summary: Cross-posting the same clips everywhere takes you to a ceiling. To break through, give the same source footage to several editors who each own a platform and cut it natively: the meat stays, the hook changes. Rank six platforms and give each editor a primary (85% of their time) and a secondary (15% experiments); on a team already getting billions of impressions this gave him a 1.5× lift. It sharpens focus, ties creative to data, builds retention through a performance flywheel, gives the audience a reason to follow you on more than one platform, and trains future leaders. Match people to platforms (TikTok: current humour; LinkedIn: deep subject knowledge; YouTube: someone who lives on YouTube). Measure with a multiplier sheet, make data the team's 'god', track only 2–4 metrics, keep a brick-by-brick list, skip the generalist 'social media manager', and reply to comments yourself.

blocks.text: the meat of the video stays roughly the same, but the entry point into the meat of the video, the hook might be different

blocks.title: Assigning platforms to editors

items.label: Rank your six platforms
items.text: Top three drive the business; bottom three get redistributed content.

items.label: Best editor
items.text: Owns platform #1 (primary) and #4 (secondary).

items.label: Second editor
items.text: Owns #2 and #5.

items.label: Third editor
items.text: Owns #3 and #6.

items.label: 85 / 15 split
items.text: 85% native content for the primary, 15% experimenting on the secondary (e.g. 'Angela': ~7 Instagram pieces + 1–2 TikTok a week).

blocks.caption: The Eye of Sauron, delegated to each editor. When Gary gave Caleb TikTok at 300K followers, his first week was 8 hours a day of scrolling and notes, no content.

blocks.label: return after switching to platform-owning editors
blocks.note: On a team already getting 'billions of impressions every year'. His analogy: at a 600–700 lb squat, 5% can be a world record.

blocks.title: The multiplier sheet (Google Sheets)

items.label: Pick a platform and format
items.text: Reels, carousels and statics each get their own benchmark.

items.label: Last 75–90 days
items.text: Take the median, not the mean: outliers skew the mean.

items.label: That median = 1.0×
items.text: Report every new post as a multiple: 150K on a 100K median = 1.5×.

items.label: Wait ~11 days
items.text: Posts increasingly 'pop' around day 7; report after the life cycle plays out.

items.label: Share across platforms
items.text: A 3× Instagram clip is a TikTok test candidate; 50K on a 10K TikTok median is a 5×.

items.label: Update monthly
items.text: The bar rises with your real performance. Directionally correct, not scientifically accurate.

blocks.caption: For YouTube he points to existing tools (1of10, ViewStats); in Feb 2025 he knew none for Instagram/TikTok.

items.label: Ideation
items.text: Research and brainstorm topics.

items.label: Creation
items.text: Script and film (batch a Thursday or Friday if real-time isn't realistic).

items.label: Editing
items.text: Optimised per platform by the platform owners.

items.label: Distribution
items.text: Post AND engage, ideally replies from you.

items.label: Analyse
items.text: Review performance, note what to improve; feeds the next ideation.

blocks.title: Data and scaling rules
items: Make data the team's 'god': ~90% of content backed by data, ~10% new ideas.
Hire (or be) the 'data nerd'.
If it doesn't change your actions, don't track it: 2–4 metrics that tell you what to do next.
Keep a brick-by-brick list of the specific things that improve your content; it becomes your training playbook.
No generalist 'social media manager': the platform owners post and manage.
Replies should be you, even if that's only ~5 a week; otherwise use a clearly labelled team account (like 'Team Gary Vee').

chapters.title: 14. Create room for experimentation
chapters.summary: Teams slowly stop experimenting once they know what works, but the algorithm never gets comfortable, and by the time a team notices it's often too late. True innovation usually has no data behind it, so experimentation has to be built into the process. His tool is a monthly or quarterly content hackathon: a safe-space day where everyone makes one or two pieces unlike their day-to-day that will either crush or flop, presents why, and the team votes for the most innovative piece to run publicly. For ongoing work he uses 70/20/10: 70% proven content, 20% small iterations, 10% pure experiments. The scaling mindset: people quit too early, it's iteration not perfection, and the audience decides what's great.

blocks.text: What got you to where you are now will not get you to the next level.

blocks.title: A content hackathon day

items.text: 15–30 min kickoff: context, and a safe space: 'I don't care how anything you make today performs.'
Make only 1–2 pieces, totally different from your normal work. Lunch is paid (gift cards) so nobody thinks about it.
Upload to a shared slide deck, one slide each.
1–1.5 h presentations: explain WHY you made it, don't just hit play.

items.label: Vote
items.text: The team votes for the most innovative piece; it runs publicly and wins a prize (e.g. an Amazon gift card).

blocks.caption: Reward innovation, not performance. He says some formats that topped their charts 'for months or even years' came from hackathons.

blocks.title: The 70/20/10 framework (base first)

items.label: 70% proven
items.text: The bread and butter: what reliably drives engagement and conversions.

items.label: 20% iterations
items.text: Small tweaks to what works: a new hook, a new CTA, a new format on the same subject.

items.label: 10% experiments
items.text: New formats, topics, messaging or creative approaches. Where breakthroughs happen.

blocks.caption: Most teams get stuck in the 70%. The best keep at least one foot in the 10% zone.

blocks.text: comfort doesn't build iconic brands.

One-person hackathon: one Saturday a month, make 1–2 reels you'd normally never post (a gym-PC crossover skit, a game-style HUD over a workout, a 'benchmark my body like a GPU' bit). Post the one you'd vote for. Week to week, run 70/20/10 loosely: for every 10 posts, about 7 proven formats, 2 with a new hook or CTA, 1 total experiment.

chapters.title: 15. Team: define the need, the role, and the job description
chapters.summary: Caleb calls the team section his favourite and arguably the most important. A team is a multiplier of the vision. Hire for culture over skills, around your platform goals, to fit your creative process, and above all to solve a real problem; a bad hire costs months and a lot of money. Define needs first by hiring for the constraint: if footage piles up unedited, hire an editor; if editors are idle, hire a videographer or strategist. Hire platform specialists (a Netflix editor isn't a YouTube editor, a brochure designer isn't a thumbnail designer), never a generalist 'social media manager', and always for the highest-impact content first. Then define the role (creating, managing or analysing? single or multi-platform? how does it serve the big picture?) and write the job description with the Four Rs, plus communication expectations and core values.

blocks.text: We hire to solve problems.

blocks.title: Hire for the bottleneck: three questions
items: What tasks take the most time away from high-value work? (A strategist spending 50% of their time editing needs an editor.)
What's slowing down execution? (Filming lots but nothing goes out → editor. Ready to edit but nothing to film → strategist/videographer.)
What content opportunities are missed due to lack of resources? (Goal of 2 YouTube videos a month, bandwidth for 1 → find the constraint.)
Prioritise bottlenecks over convenience: hire for leverage, not to offload busywork.

left.title: Looks qualified
items: Netflix/commercial film editor
Documentary DP
Brochure/logo graphic designer
Generalist social media manager
Generic copywriter

right.title: Actually fits
items: YouTube editor
Run-and-gun vlog shooter
Thumbnail designer (YouTube best practices 'slap in the face' of traditional design)
Channel-specific owner / platform strategist
LinkedIn writer

blocks.text: If they're a generalist, if they are great at all of the platforms, they suck at all of the platforms.

blocks.title: The Four Rs job description (+2)

items.label: Role
items.text: The contribution and function on the team.

items.label: Responsibilities
items.text: What they own daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly (the input).

items.label: Requirements
items.text: Skills and experience, e.g. 'three plus years of experience growing a personal brand'.

items.label: Results
items.text: Specific outputs (the output), e.g. 'a minimum of two videos per month'; LinkedIn 'at least two written and two video posts per week'.

items.label: + Communication & cadence
items.text: Say it up front if you expect a 7:30 a.m. Slack reply.

items.label: + Core values
items.text: They should already live by them.

blocks.caption: 'What do you get with vague job descriptions? Vague candidates.'

blocks.text: At your stage the 'team' is you, maybe a friend or a freelancer. Use the bottleneck test anyway: if you film plenty but posts stall in editing, your first paid help is an editor for simple trims and captions; if you edit fast but run out of ideas, it's an hour a week with someone who helps you script. And write even a one-paragraph brief with the four Rs, especially Results: '3 reels a week, delivered by Friday'.

chapters.title: 16. The hiring funnel, tryouts and culture fit
chapters.summary: Every hiring mistake Caleb made came from rushing and ignoring red flags; the funnel is designed to surface them. You're looking for an 80% candidate and asking whether the missing 20% is trainable or unnecessary. The six steps are application (CV plus an optional video), screening call, technical interview, technical assessment, culture interview and final interview, and a one-person team can combine steps. For editors, designers and strategists he also runs a tryout funnel with the assessment first. He hires for mindset over polish, with Trevor (6/10 editing, 10/10 culture) and Jason (took blunt feedback gratefully) as examples. He ends with what fits, and what's a red flag, for TikTok/Instagram, LinkedIn and YouTube.

blocks.title: The six-step hiring funnel

items.label: Application
items.text: CV plus an OPTIONAL video: personality never shows in a CV, and the video filters out mass/AI appliers. 10 jobs in 5 years = explore it, not auto-reject.

items.label: Screening call
items.text: Salary, location, communication and travel expectations, plus 2–3 light technical questions (which also expose AI-fed answers).

items.label: Technical interview
items.text: Strategic knowledge AND execution: 'How would you innovate on our current style?' He wants to see how they think, not a checklist follower.

items.label: Technical assessment
items.text: Mirrors the real job, same for every candidate: e.g. 72 hours + ~1 hour of raw footage to create a new short-form style.

items.label: Culture interview
items.text: Real scenarios: direct feedback in front of 5+ people, a non-manager demanding your time, a terse CEO.

items.label: Final interview
items.text: With the most senior person they'll work with; closes every open question. Their questions to you reveal a lot.

blocks.caption: Why it works: removes bad hires early, checks platform fit ('Are they a great editor or are they a great YouTube editor?'), checks culture, and speeds hiring up.

blocks.title: The tryout funnel (editors, designers, strategists)

items.label: Monday
items.text: Announce tryouts and open registration.

items.label: Thursday 12 p.m. PT
items.text: Registration closes.

items.label: Thursday ~5 p.m.
items.text: Email the raw footage and brief: a 12–20 min YouTube edit + thumbnail + title + a short.

items.label: Monday 9 a.m.
items.text: Deadline. How they prioritise is part of the test.

items.label: Then
items.text: Screening → technical interview → culture → final.

blocks.caption: His claim: ~1,500 registered, ~220–250 submitted. Only works when one shared source asset can scale to hundreds of people (not for videographers).

blocks.title: Culture vs skill: who he hires

items.label: Hire and train
items.text: Strong culture, mid skill. Skills can be trained fast (5–6/10 → 8–9/10). His Trevor case.

items.label: Rare: hire now
items.text: Strong culture and strong skill.

items.label: Pass
items.text: Weak on both.

items.label: The anchor
items.text: Great skill, ego, can't take feedback. Drags everyone down: 'an anchor rather than a rocket'.

blocks.caption: Our 2×2 of his stated preference: culture 5–6 → 8–9 is far harder to train than editing skill.

blocks.title: Trevor and Jason
blocks.text: Caleb hired Trevor Odum about three years before filming at roughly '6 out of 10' as an editor but '10 out of 10' on culture: humble, eager, took the boring tasks too. Trevor later became lead editor. Jason came through the tryout with an edit that wasn't top-10, but when Caleb gave blunt feedback (a dropped frame, a missing plugin) Jason thanked him for it. He became one of Caleb's best hires.
Hire for mindset and train for execution.

left.title: What fits
items: TikTok/IG: lives on the apps, fast-paced editing, opens and closes loops to hold attention, spots gaps in your niche
LinkedIn: concise high-value writing that sparks conversation in the comments
YouTube: nails the opening 15–30 s, builds tension and open loops, spreads value through the video (watch time)

right.title: Red flags
items: TikTok/IG: obsessed with production value without understanding the hook
LinkedIn: formal, corporate, stiff writing; human and personable stands out
YouTube videographer: stops every scene for perfect light, refuses zooms ('only use primes') on a run-and-gun vlog

chapters.title: 17. Start lean, contractors vs full-time, onboarding
chapters.summary: Avoid over-hiring: a small 'SEAL Team Six' team of specialists who can wear several hats beats a bloated one. It avoids payroll before content ROI is proven, keeps you nimble (speedboat vs oil tanker), builds shared context and gives cover when someone is sick or leaves. Grow roles in three steps: multi-role hires, document the process, specialise as you scale (an editor pulled out to film loses another 30–45 minutes getting back into flow). He compares full-time employees and contractors/agencies on six factors and gives three growth stages. Then onboarding: a 30-60-90 plan (ideally sent before day one), materials, a mentor, frequent short check-ins, an onboarding hub, clear ownership and KPIs. Good onboarding speeds ramp-up, improves retention and builds initiative.

items.label: Start with multi-role hires
items.text: E.g. one person who films and edits; decide which skill matters more right now.

items.label: Document and define the process
items.text: Every workflow written down so the next person can pick it up.

items.label: Specialise as you scale
items.text: Hire the editor; the shooter goes back to only filming. Protect flow.

blocks.title: Full-time employee vs contractor/agency (his six factors)

left.title: Full-time employee
items: Budget: higher long-term cost (salary, benefits, training)
Workload: ongoing daily tasks
Expertise: deep knowledge; you invest in training them
Speed: 60–90 days to ramp up, then continuity
Brand consistency: easier, they're in internal meetings
Scalability: grows into leaders who carry the team's DNA

right.title: Contractor / agency
items: Budget: cheaper for short-term or specialist work; arrives 'batteries included'
Workload: project-based, flexible, temporary (filming twice a month, an event)
Expertise: should arrive as the expert; 3–6 months of an agency = a 'fast pass'
Speed: immediate, but agencies churn (~7 editors in 6–12 months)
Brand consistency: needs the most oversight
Scalability: best for testing a theory before a full-time hire

blocks.title: Three growth stages (general advice, not doctrine)

items.label: Year 0–1
items.text: Mostly contractors and agencies. Stay lean, test which platforms are best FOR YOU. Founder heavily involved in content and strategy.

items.label: Years 1–3
items.text: Bring critical roles in-house (e.g. YouTube brings 70–80% of qualified leads → in-house editor). Shrink the agency to consulting, ideation, scripting, packaging.

items.label: Year 3+
items.text: All critical, high-volume roles in-house; speed and communication jump. Keep agencies for specialist work, platform relationships (e.g. Meta reps) and temporary sprints.

items.label: Days 1–30
items.text: Orientation and core learning: vision, values, workflows, tools, small tasks for early wins, regular check-ins. An editor shadows a senior editor and studies the top 5 videos and why they worked.

items.label: Days 31–60
items.text: Ownership: executes core responsibilities independently, builds their own workflow inside the team process; work and communication get reviewed.

items.label: Days 61–90
items.text: Full integration with minimal supervision; results against KPIs (e.g. watch time vs average, rate of progress).

items.label: Day 90 review
items.text: Praise specifics; correct anything that can't continue, now.

blocks.text: If you do not tell them now and they continue doing it, that is not their fault. That is your fault.

blocks.title: Onboarding beyond the 30-60-90
items: Send a clear plan and materials before day one (handbook, vision deck, strategy deck).
Assign a mentor or onboarding buddy.
Month one: three 10-minute check-ins (Mon/Wed/Fri) instead of one long meeting.
Celebrate early wins, like speaking up in a meeting on day one.
Bonus: an onboarding hub, even just a Google Drive folder.
Keep role descriptions updated; never leave two people 'owning' the same task without clarity. Set KPIs.
Why: faster ramp-up, retention (losing someone costs ~2.5× what they cost, his figure), more initiative.

chapters.title: 18. Developing and retaining the team
chapters.summary: A team that stops evolving is just maintaining. Caleb's first tool is a culture of ownership instead of a 'checklist army' that only follows SOPs: don't solve their problems, ask how they'd handle it if you were gone, have them bring solutions rather than problems, and let non-critical mistakes happen. Teaching is his leadership hack: rotating, team-led weekly trainings build mastery, because if you can't explain it you don't fully understand it, and they reveal hidden strengths. He pairs people in a mentorship loop by skill, not tenure. He aligns work with each person's long-term goals through one-on-ones, promotes specialisation (Trevor chose to stay in short form and became lead editor at 22–23), and turns paid workshops into team trainings. His takeaways: push ownership down, make teaching a habit, tie their growth to the company's, go deep not wide, and hold structured check-ins.

blocks.text: If you are the only one making decisions, you don't have a team.

items.label: Don't solve it for them
items.text: Ask: 'How would you handle this if I got hit by a bus / was out three weeks?'

items.label: Solutions, not problems
items.text: Move them from 'how do I solve this?' to 'which of these two or three would you try?'

items.label: Flip it again
items.text: Ask which of their options they think is best.

items.label: Autonomy with accountability
items.text: If it's not mission-critical, let them try the idea you suspect won't work. No fear → creativity.

blocks.title: Three months of answering texts
blocks.text: A brilliant creative director kept texting Caleb mid-shoot asking how to handle the talent. Caleb always answered, and after three months the questions came just as often. When he switched to 'How would you handle this?', the director sometimes chose wrong (risking a shoot), but learned, and now leads that relationship without texting him.

blocks.title: Teaching reveals real understanding (an editing example he gives)
blocks.before: Why did you cut 12 frames, 36 frames, 12, 36? 'It felt right.'
blocks.after: I trained the audience to expect that cadence, because the next scene was dramatic and I was going to break the pattern. Breaking a trained rhythm emphasises the moment.
blocks.why: If you can't explain it, you don't fully understand it. Team-led trainings force the explanation and show who's secretly great at sound design or storytelling.

blocks.title: One-on-one questions he uses
items: What's your long-term career goal?
Where do you see yourself after this role?
What skills do you want to develop? (An editor into motion graphics gets fancier lower thirds, transitions, text animation.)
How's your workload? What's slowing you down? Can I bulldoze any roadblocks?
What have you wanted to learn but not had time for?
Then send 1–2 people to a paid workshop and have them turn it into a team training.

blocks.text: If you choose not to make time for feedback, you'll eventually have to make time for hiring.

chapters.title: 19. Team culture: values, transparency, schedules, remote vs hybrid
chapters.summary: Good culture isn't built by accident; it's the team's operating system. Define core values, then hire on them, publicly reward actions that reflect them, and lead by example (his youth pastor: whatever you do, they'll do ten times). Patagonia is his example of values actually lived. Be transparent about decisions (he explained why a six-day, 13-hour-a-day edit was killed), own mistakes immediately, and communicate pivots early. Care about people outside work (a Lego set for a birthday, soup when someone is sick), and give stretch opportunities, because trust begets trust. Protect makers with Paul Graham's maker/manager schedule. On remote vs in-person vs hybrid he compares six factors: hybrid is best if you can afford it, in-person is best for the company, and remote is best for the employee. He closes the section: lead with empathy, not fear.

blocks.title: Reinforcing core values
items: Hire on values alignment, not just skill.
Recognise and reward value-aligned actions publicly (Slack shout-outs, team meetups, awards).
Lead by example: slow replies, late arrivals or PJs on calls get copied ×10.
Explain the why behind decisions, own your mistakes first, and announce pivots as early as possible.
Show care outside work; give stretch opportunities, because trust begets trust.

blocks.title: His maker/manager week (credited to Paul Graham)

items.label: Every day
items.text: Maker time 7 a.m.–12 p.m. (no meetings for makers); manager time 12–5 p.m.

items.label: Monday
items.text: Meeting day: stack as many calls as possible.

items.label: Tue / Thu / Fri
items.text: Maker mornings, manager time roughly 2–5 p.m.

items.label: Wednesday
items.text: Full maker day, blocked entirely.

blocks.caption: One interruption costs a maker 30 minutes to an hour of flow. Teams tend to push for a full maker day once they have this.

blocks.text: You are both maker and manager. Give your filming/editing block a fixed slot at your best-energy time (his 'energy rhythm'), with notifications off, and push DMs, comment replies and brand emails into a separate 'manager' window.

blocks.title: Remote vs in-person (hybrid sits between on most factors)

left.title: Remote
items: Flexibility: very high; can justify below-market pay
Collaboration: needs clear tools and rules; few happy accidents
Productivity: depends on the person
Cost: cheapest
Talent pool: the whole world, without LA/NYC premiums
Culture: hardest; use morning check-ins and occasional meetups

right.title: In-person
items: Flexibility: low, fixed hours and location
Collaboration: easiest; real-time back-and-forth beats Frame.io notes
Productivity: depends on the person (shoulder taps)
Cost: highest: rent, utilities, perks (hybrid is worst here: paying for half-empty space)
Talent pool: limited outside creative hubs; relocation premium
Culture: easiest, but more drama with younger post-COVID hires

blocks.text: In person is best for the company. remote is best for the employee.
Lead your team with empathy, not fear.

chapters.title: 20. Monetise: trust before transactions
chapters.summary: Most people monetise too early and wonder why nobody buys; trust comes before the transaction. Caleb admits the temptation (he and Trevor ran the numbers on charging for this course) and accepts that bills sometimes force earlier selling. Before monetising, give an unbelievable amount of value, demonstrate credibility, and build a relationship. Choose from five models, and look in your DMs and comments for what people already ask for. Share the knowledge and sell the execution, build an offer stack starting with a single offer, let content do the selling (a soft CTA built on a result), and play the long game: give the real frameworks, build recurring series people binge 'like Netflix', and protect your reputation by asking whether each move increases or decreases trust. He closes with a recap of every module, an invitation to apply to his firm, a 'send it to your team or a friend' CTA, and thanks.

items.label: Give unbelievable value up front
items.text: They should feel they're winning before they ever spend money.

items.label: Demonstrate credibility and expertise
items.text: Become the go-to authority.

items.label: Establish a relationship
items.text: Engagement matters. If people feel they know you, sales need no fake scarcity or urgency.

blocks.title: Five monetisation models
items: Services: agency, consulting, coaching. High-touch; fits deep expertise people already ask you for.
Products: digital (ebooks, templates, playbooks, courses; very high margin, lean here early) or physical (books, apparel).
Affiliates and sponsorships: only what you actually use and believe in, or the pairing creates a 'bad brand effect'.
Community and memberships: recurring revenue, a hub for super-fans.
Ads and content monetisation: small at first; pair it with another model.
Pro tip: read your email, DMs and comments for what people already want.

blocks.title: The Harley exhaust
blocks.text: Caleb watched about 100 YouTube videos on swapping the exhaust on his Harley Road King. He learned exactly what to buy, and realised he's not mechanical and it was too expensive a bike to mess up. So he paid the Harley dealership, which had put out free content showing how, to install it. They gave away the knowledge and sold the execution.

blocks.title: The offer stack (base first; start with ONE offer)

items.label: Free content
items.text: Builds trust and awareness.

items.label: Lead magnet
items.text: Mini-course, SOP, checklist or playbook that captures emails/phone numbers, so you're not beholden to algorithms.

items.label: Low ticket: $10–100
items.text: Ebooks, mini-courses, templates. Removes the barrier to entry.

items.label: Mid ticket: $500–5,000
items.text: Group coaching, memberships, in-depth courses.

items.label: High ticket: $10,000+
items.text: 1:1 consulting, agency, done-for-you. Few brands start here.

blocks.caption: 'Don't start with five different offers. You're going to confuse your audience.'

blocks.title: Let content do the selling
blocks.before: Buy my ebook on personal branding.
blocks.after: I helped John go from 0 to 10k followers in 4 and 1/2 months using this exact strategy. If you want the full system, I break it down in my ebook. There's a link in my bio.
blocks.why: People hate feeling sold to but love buying from someone they trust. A result plus a soft CTA does the persuading. (John is his illustrative example.)

blocks.text: It is way harder to rebuild trust than it is to maintain trust.

production.detail: The course opens with a two-path frame (forgettable vs intentional brand), names a pain ('you've probably hit a ceiling') and a promise ('save you years and hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of mistakes') inside the first ~35 seconds.
Four announced sections (branding, content, team, monetise) with a spoken roadmap at 0:50 and a full module-by-module recap at 6:19:35. Two mid-roll ads for his own newsletter (2:07:33, 4:38:16).

Talking head shot on three cameras, with deliberate set, lighting, framing and audio (his own description at 1:35:05). Trevor behind camera nods and gives thumbs-ups as live feedback. Visuals were not seen for this module.

He says on-screen icons pop up to point to downloadable worksheets and playbooks (job description, FTE vs contractor sheet, maker/manager playbook, remote/hybrid sheet). A contractor, Michael, does the motion graphics. We don't have the sheets.

Recorded on location with passing semis and police sirens left in: 'perfect is the enemy of posted'. Voice technique he names: speed up then slow down, loud then quiet, to flag emphasis (a pattern interrupt).
Long-form education, 6 h 22 min, in ~40 modules of 5–25 minutes each, each opened with a plain 'next section is…' signpost and often closed with a summary list.

He practises his own advice: admits insecurity ('I feel like I look fat'), uncertainty about whether the course will pay off, and failures (pay cut, firing friends), and keeps saying 'do more of what I say… not as much of what I do'.
No sales push inside the teaching. The close asks you to download the playbooks, apply to his firm if you want help, and share it ('sending it to your team on Slack or texting it to a friend').

takeaways.text: Brand = an intentional pairing of relevant things done consistently; the audience then makes the association by itself.
Work backwards: desired outcome → what to be known for → what to do → what to learn today.
Decide what you will NOT be associated with (sponsors, collabs, podcasts); awareness isn't worth the wrong pairing.
Positioning = own the gap: what do creators in your space say that you disagree with?
Tell the story behind the trait instead of claiming the trait.
Brand story = catalyst + core truth + proof, repeated.
Start narrow, expand into adjacent topics in layers, not leaps.
80% core topic, 20% other interests: interest stacking gives viewers more at bats to connect.
Two or three platforms, one in focus at a time (Eye of Sauron).
Short form builds awareness; long form converts.
The audience defines quality: expand volume to learn, then compress into more effort per piece.
Perfect is the enemy of posted; start from a baseline you can sustain.
Waterfall: mine one long piece into 10+ platform pieces, and use a winner on one platform to seed others.
Carousels: hook on slide 1 AND slide 2, one simple image + 1–2 sentences per slide.
Review the top 10% of the last 90 days every month and copy only what all of them share.
Benchmark with a multiplier sheet: median of 75–90 days = 1.0×, report each post as a multiple after ~11 days.
Hook window: 2–3 s on short form, 15–20 s max on YouTube long form.
Story structure: hook → problem → journey (messy middle) → lesson → CTA.
Keep retelling your origin story; every post meets a cold audience.
Answer the objections from your comments inside your content.
Ideas come from repeated DM/comment questions, not 'what should I make?' polls.
Reply to the people already commenting yourself; use niche inside jokes.
Same footage, native edit per platform: the meat stays, the hook changes.
70/20/10: proven, iterations, pure experiments.
Track only the 2–4 metrics that change what you do next; optimise for conversions.
Trust before transactions: share the knowledge, sell the execution.
Offer ladder: free → lead magnet → low → mid → high ticket, one offer first.
Hire for the bottleneck and for platform specialists, culture over skill.

glossary.def: A pairing of things. Good branding is an intentional pairing of relevant things done consistently.
The byproduct of branding: the association the audience makes on its own when it hears your name.
Four questions worked backwards: desired outcome, known for, do, learn.
Something you deliberately refuse to be paired with (a sponsor, a collab, a podcast), because repeated pairing creates the association anyway.
What's missing in your space (information, philosophy, or personality) that you can own.
Caleb's three-part brand story: why you exist, what you believe that others don't, and the repeated evidence.
Expand into adjacent topics gradually so each step feels natural to the audience.
Spending ~20% of content on your other interests so viewers have more 'at bats' to connect with you.
A chance for a viewer to find something in common with you (baseball metaphor).
The one content medium (written, video, audio, visual) you lean into most.
His word for rambling down idea rabbit-trails on camera; fixed by a better editor, not by avoiding video.
Focus on one of your 2–3 platforms at a time while the others run in maintenance mode, then rotate.
Posting enough to keep the existing audience engaged on a platform without trying to grow it.
Expand volume to learn what the audience calls quality, then compress into fewer, higher-effort pieces.
A long piece (YouTube video, newsletter, deep thread) that other pieces are mined from.
Going through pillar content for self-contained moments, quotes and summaries worth posting on their own.
Turning one pillar piece into many platform pieces (clips, quotes, posts, carousels); credited to Gary Vee.
Monthly review of your best 10% of posts from the last 90 days to find the one or two traits all of them share.
The same message remade for each platform's needs instead of identical cross-posts.
Using what performed on one platform/medium to inform new content in another (tweet → short → poster → LinkedIn → YouTube).
Reading replies, DMs and comments for repeated questions or strong reactions, then acting on them fast.
Something unexpected that breaks the viewer's autopilot: an odd opening, or a change in speaking pace or volume.
The doubts, low points and uncertainty in the journey part of a story; what makes it relatable.
A sales video that answers objections before the sales call; Caleb wants content to answer objections the same way.
User-generated content: the audience's own posts, which you can stitch or feature.
Benchmark = median performance of the last 75–90 days per platform and format; each post is reported as a multiple of it.
A running internal list of specific things that improve your content results; becomes a training playbook.
A monthly or quarterly day where everyone makes 1–2 radically new pieces, presents why, and the team votes on the most innovative.
70% proven content, 20% small iterations, 10% pure experiments.
A team that only follows SOPs and instructions without ownership or innovation.
Job description structure: Role, Responsibilities, Requirements, Results.
Hiring by giving every registrant the same raw footage and brief first, then interviewing the best submissions.
Onboarding in three 30-day phases: learn, own, fully integrate, ending with a review.
Paul Graham's idea: makers need long uninterrupted blocks, managers work in meetings, so separate the two in the calendar.

glossary.term: Share the knowledge, sell the execution
glossary.def: Give the real frameworks free; people pay for help doing it.
Free content → lead magnet → low ticket → mid ticket → high ticket, built up one offer at a time.
A free checklist, playbook or mini-course traded for an email or phone number, so you own a direct line to your audience.

quiz.q: What are Caleb's three ingredients of good branding, and what is 'brand'?
quiz.a: An intentional pairing of relevant things done consistently. Brand is the byproduct: the audience inherently associating those things together.

quiz.q: List the four Brand Journey questions in order. Which one gives you day-one actions?
quiz.a: Desired outcome → what do I have to be known for → what do I have to do → what do I have to learn. The last (learn) gives day-one actions.

quiz.q: Which question does Caleb call more important than 'what do I want to be associated with'?
quiz.a: What do I NOT want to be associated with? (anti-associations)

quiz.q: Give his two questions for finding a positioning gap.
quiz.a: What are creators in my space saying that I disagree with? How can I bring a fresh perspective to what has been taught for years?

quiz.q: What are the three parts of his brand story framework?
quiz.a: Catalyst (why you exist), Core truth (what you believe that others don't), Proof (repeated evidence through actions).

quiz.q: When does he say it's OK to expand into a new topic?
quiz.a: When you're truly excellent at it, the current topic gets consistent engagement, the new topic is adjacent, or the audience asks for something you've hinted at. Expand in layers, not leaps.

quiz.q: What is the Eye of Sauron approach?
quiz.a: Of your 2–3 platforms, focus resources on one while the others sit in maintenance mode, then rotate.

quiz.q: In the accordion method, who decides what quality is, and what do you do once you know?
quiz.a: The audience decides. Then you compress: fewer pieces with more effort each, built on what they responded to.

quiz.q: Why do both slide 1 and slide 2 of a carousel need a hook?
quiz.a: If someone doesn't engage, Instagram re-serves the carousel to followers starting on slide 2 (Feb 2025 observation).

quiz.q: Why does he prefer one 1M-view video to four 250K-view videos?
quiz.a: Same views, not the same eyeballs: 60–70% of the 250K videos' views came from the existing audience, while the 1M video reached mostly new people.

quiz.q: How do you build a multiplier-sheet benchmark, and how long do you wait before reporting?
quiz.a: Median (not mean) of the last 75–90 days per platform and format; report each post as a multiple after ~11 days; update monthly.

quiz.q: What are the five steps of his storytelling framework?
quiz.a: Hook, Problem, Journey, Lesson, CTA.

quiz.q: How long is the hook window on short form vs YouTube long form?
quiz.a: About 2–3 seconds on short form; about 15–20 seconds max on long form (the industry says 30).

quiz.q: Why should you keep telling your origin story even when you're bored of it?
quiz.a: Treat content as if it always reaches a cold audience; new viewers don't know it, and origin stories are what people resonate with most.

quiz.q: Why does he dislike 'what should I make next?' polls?
quiz.a: Too open-ended ('blue ocean'), and people don't know what they need. Use the questions they already send in DMs and comments.

quiz.q: What does 70/20/10 stand for?
quiz.a: 70% proven content, 20% small iterations (new hook, CTA or format), 10% pure experiments.

quiz.q: What is the rule for deciding which metrics to track?
quiz.a: If it doesn't change your actions, don't track it. Track 2–4 metrics that tell you what to do next.

quiz.q: Name the Four Rs of a job description.
quiz.a: Role, Responsibilities, Requirements, Results (plus communication expectations and core values).

quiz.q: Which candidate does Caleb prefer: strong culture/mid skill or high skill/big ego?
quiz.a: Strong culture and mid skill. Skills train fast, culture doesn't; 'Hire for mindset and train for execution.'

quiz.q: What does 'share the knowledge, sell the execution' mean, using his Harley story?
quiz.a: Give the real know-how free; people realise doing it is hard and pay you to execute. He watched ~100 exhaust videos, then paid the dealership to install it.

quiz.q: What question should you ask before any monetisation move?
quiz.a: Will this increase trust with my audience or decrease it? If it decreases trust, it isn't worth it.

try_it.title: Fill in your Brand Journey
steps: Write your desired outcome for the next 12 months in one sentence (e.g. a follower target, a first paid brand deal, a YouTube channel).
Write the one thing you'd need to be known for to get there (e.g. 'the funny guy who actually knows lifting and PCs').
List 3 actions that would make you known for it (weekly series, monthly build, PR log).
List what you'd need to learn first (scripting hooks, a new edit style, LinkedIn writing). That's your to-do list this week.

try_it.title: Write your anti-association list
steps: List 5 kinds of sponsors, collabs or trends you'd refuse even for a big audience (betting apps, shady supplements, fake giveaways, rage-bait duets).
For each, write the association it would create in a viewer's head.
Pin the list in your notes and check every brand DM against it before replying.

try_it.title: Find your gap in 20 minutes
steps: Watch 10 top reels in gym and PC content.
Write 3 things they say that you disagree with or would say differently.
Turn each into a contrarian hook: state the trope, then your view (e.g. 'You don't need a ₹2 lakh PC for 1440p. Here's what you need.').
Film the strongest one this week.

try_it.title: Interest-stack calendar
steps: Pick your 80% core (gym, tech or gaming) and keep it for 8 weeks.
Plan 10 posts: 8 on the core, 2 on the other interests or a crossover (e.g. 'rating gym equipment like PC parts').
After 8 weeks, compare engagement on the core vs crossover posts before changing the mix.

try_it.title: Two-week accordion sprint
steps: For 14 days, post one lightly edited reel a day: iPhone 15 on the tripod, trimmed, captions only.
Log each post's views, saves, shares and comment questions in a sheet.
On day 15, find the 2 best posts and what they share (topic, hook type, length).
Compress: for the next two weeks post 3 a week, each with full effort on that winning pattern.

try_it.title: Waterfall one PC build
steps: Film one long piece (5–10 min): e.g. a budget build or a setup tour.
Mine it: 3–4 clips with the most opinionated moments, 2 quote lines, 1 written post from the transcript.
Make a listicle carousel: 2 slides per section, 1 image + 1–2 sentences per slide, a hook on slide 1 and on slide 2.
Re-cut the hook per platform (Reels vs Shorts) instead of posting the identical file everywhere.
Count the pieces; aim for 10.

try_it.title: Build your multiplier sheet
steps: Export your last 90 days of reels: date, views, likes, comments, shares, saves, follows.
Take the median views: that's 1.0×.
For each new reel, wait ~11 days, then write views ÷ median (e.g. 3,000 on a 1,200 median = 2.5×).
Monthly: list the top 10% and write the one or two things all of them share; update the median.

try_it.title: Inside-joke + reply month
steps: Write a lexicon of 10 phrases your gym, PC and gaming viewers already use.
Invent one sign-off or running joke that's only yours and use it in every post.
For 30 days, personally reply to every comment within 24 hours.
Each week, note repeated questions from comments/DMs and answer the top one in a reel, without saying 'many of you asked'.

try_it.title: Origin story in five beats
steps: Hook: one bold line about how you started (2–3 s).
Problem: the specific, relatable stakes (where you were stuck).
Journey: one low point and one doubt, the messy middle.
Lesson: 2–3 steps a viewer can copy today.
CTA: 'comment the one thing you'll try this week'. Keep this reel and re-post a fresh version every few months for new followers.

try_it.title: Monthly solo hackathon
steps: Block one Saturday a month, phone on do-not-disturb.
Make 1–2 pieces unlike anything you've posted (a game-HUD overlay on a workout, a skit, a new format).
Write one line on WHY each might work.
Post the one you'd vote for and track its multiplier, but judge the day on novelty, not views.

try_it.title: Sketch your future offer stack
steps: From DMs and comments, list what people already ask you for (a beginner program, a PC parts list, settings).
Turn the most-asked one into a free lead magnet (e.g. a PDF build checklist) that collects emails.
Write, but don't launch yet, one low-ticket idea (₹299–999 template or program).
Before any deal or launch, ask: will this increase or decrease trust?
